question.prompt:
The convex pentagon \(ABCDE\) has \(\angle A=\angle B=120^\circ,\) \(EA=AB=BC=2\) and \(CD=DE=4.\) What is the area of \(ABCDE?\)

[Figure 1](figures/1993_AMC_12_Q14_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Draw diagonal \(CE\). It splits the convex pentagon into quadrilateral \(ABCE\) and triangle \(CDE\). The two \(120^\circ\) angles will let us find \(CE\) and show that \(ABCE\) is a trapezoid.

Place \(AB\) horizontally, with the pentagon above it. Drop perpendiculars from \(E\) and \(C\) to the line \(AB\), meeting it at \(P\) and \(Q\), respectively. Since the angles at \(A\) and \(B\) are \(120^\circ\), \(P\) lies to the left of \(A\), \(Q\) lies to the right of \(B\), and each resulting right triangle has angles \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\). Each has hypotenuse \(2\), so the leg opposite \(30^\circ\) is \(1\). Consequently,
\[
AP=BQ=1,\qquad
EP=CQ=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3.
\]
The equal perpendicular heights show that \(CE\parallel AB\), and
\[
CE=AP+AB+BQ=1+2+1=4.
\]
Thus trapezoid \(ABCE\) has area
\[
\frac{AB+CE}{2}\cdot EP
=\frac{2+4}{2}\sqrt3=3\sqrt3.
\]
Since \(CD=DE=CE=4\), triangle \(CDE\) is equilateral. Its altitude bisects \(CE\), so its height is
\[
\sqrt{4^2-2^2}=2\sqrt3.
\]
Its area is therefore \(\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot2\sqrt3=4\sqrt3\). The diagonal partitions the pentagon without overlapping interiors, so its total area is
\[
3\sqrt3+4\sqrt3=\boxed{7\sqrt3},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Split into a trapezoid and a triangle

solutions.explanation:
The \(120^\circ\) angles suggest extending \(EA\) beyond \(A\) and \(CB\) beyond \(B\). Let the extended rays meet at \(F\). Each ray makes a \(60^\circ\) angle with \(AB\) on the side below it, so they meet there and form
\[
\angle FAB=\angle ABF=60^\circ.
\]
The third angle is also \(60^\circ\), making \(\triangle FAB\) equilateral. Hence \(AF=BF=AB=2\).

Now \(EF=EA+AF=4\) and \(CF=CB+BF=4\). Also \(\angle EFC=\angle AFB=60^\circ\). Thus the isosceles triangle \(EFC\) has all three angles equal to \(60^\circ\), so it is equilateral and \(EC=4\). Since \(CD=DE=4\), triangle \(CDE\) is equilateral too. Convexity places \(D\) on the opposite side of \(CE\) from \(A\), \(B\), and \(F\).

Together, triangles \(EFC\) and \(CDE\) fill a larger quadrilateral. Removing triangle \(FAB\) leaves exactly pentagon \(ABCDE\). To calculate these areas, an equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has an altitude that bisects its base, giving height
\[
\sqrt{s^2-(s/2)^2}=\frac{s\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Its area is therefore \(s^2\sqrt3/4\). Applying this to the two side-4 triangles and the side-2 triangle gives
\[
\operatorname{Area}(ABCDE)
=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(4^2+4^2-2^2)
=\boxed{7\sqrt3}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
